title: Why does HCF times LCM equal the product?
description: Twelve and eighteen are broken into primes. For each prime, the smaller count goes to the highest common factor and the larger count to the lowest common multiple, so together they use exactly the primes of the product. Keeko doubts this and gives the highest common factor the larger count.
teaching_notes: One idea: the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple share out the primes of the two numbers, so their product equals the product of the numbers. Watch for students who give the highest common factor the larger count of each prime.

source: Explain with 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3 why HCF × LCM equals the product.
video_script.why: The child has seen that the highest common factor times the lowest common multiple equals the product and now sees why, using primes.
video_script.substitution: Count each prime in both numbers, give the smaller count to the highest common factor and the larger count to the lowest common multiple.
video_script.anchor: The prime factorisations of twelve and eighteen written one under the other, with the primes in columns.
video_script.wrong_answer: the highest common factor takes the larger count of each prime
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko gives the highest common factor two twos and two threes, which makes thirty six, the same as the lowest common multiple.
video_script.payoff_line: Together the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple use exactly the primes of the product

final_answer.value: Each prime's smaller count goes to the HCF and its larger count to the LCM, so together they use exactly the primes of the product: 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18
final_answer.spoken: the smaller count of each prime goes to the highest common factor and the larger count goes to the lowest common multiple, so together they use exactly the primes of the product

hold_back: Each prime's smaller count goes to the HCF and its larger count to the LCM
never_show: 36 as the highest common factor of 12 and 18, marked right
maths_rules: prime 2: counts 2 and 1; HCF takes 1, LCM takes 2; together 3 twos, as in the product
prime 3: counts 1 and 2; HCF takes 1, LCM takes 2; together 3 threes, as in the product
slip: if the HCF took the larger counts it would be 36 and 36 × 36 = 1296, not 216

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We take twelve and eighteen.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The largest number that divides both numbers is called their highest common factor.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The smallest number that is a multiple of both is called their lowest common multiple.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>Why does the highest common factor times the lowest common multiple equal the product of the two numbers?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Every number can be broken into primes, which are numbers whose only factors are one and itself.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twelve is two times two times three, and eighteen is two times three times three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>We count how many times each prime appears in each number.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: prime 2. Counts 2 and 1. HCF takes 1, LCM takes 2. Together 3 twos; the product has 2 + 1 = 3 twos

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, look at the prime two. Twelve has two twos, and eighteen has one.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The highest common factor takes one two. The lowest common multiple takes two twos.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Together that is three twos. The product also has two plus one, which is three twos.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: prime 3. Counts 1 and 2. HCF takes 1, LCM takes 2. Together 3 threes; the product has 1 + 2 = 3 threes

marks.m1: the column of 3s is lit with counts 1 and 2
marks.m2: one 3 is sent to the HCF box and two 3s to the LCM box
marks.m3: 3 threes are counted and set beside the 3 threes of the product

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, look at the prime three. Twelve has one three, and eighteen has two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The highest common factor takes one three. The lowest common multiple takes two threes.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Together that is three threes, and the product also has three threes.

marks.m1: the primes in the HCF box are joined as 2 × 3 = 6
marks.m2: the primes in the LCM box are joined as 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, the highest common factor is two times three, which is six.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The lowest common multiple is two times two times three times three, which is thirty six.

marks.m2: 12 × 18 = 216 is written beside it and an equals sign joins them

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, six times thirty six is two hundred sixteen.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twelve times eighteen is also two hundred sixteen, so they match.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the highest common factor takes the larger count of each prime. That gives two twos and two threes.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But that makes thirty six, which is the lowest common multiple.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Thirty six times thirty six is one thousand two hundred ninety six, far more than two hundred sixteen.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. It takes the smaller count.
